newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: U.S. human rights envoy warns Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: U.S. human rights envoy warns Milosevic.

text.p: A U.S. envoy warned Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Thursday that only more cooperation with the U.N. war crimes tribunal could bring Yugoslavia back into the world community.

"International financial assistance and access to international organisations like...the United Nations, depends on much, much more cooperation with the tribunal," Assistant Secretary of State for Human Rights John Shattuck told reporters in Belgrade as he ended a tour of Bosnia, Croatia and Serbian-dominated Yugoslavia.
The International War crimes Tribunal for former Yugoslavia in The Hague has indicted more than 70 people from former Yugoslavia, most of them Bosnian Serbs.
But it has only seven suspects in its custody. The others, including former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and his military commander General Ratko Mladic, remain free.
Shattuck said he had made clear to Milosevic that cooperation with the tribunal and freedom of the press are "in the forefront of U.S. policy" over Serbia.
The U.S. official said Milosevic agreed that war criminals should be prosecuted but argued that Yugoslavia's constitution forbade extradition of its citizens to foreign countries.
"That should not be an obstacle since the war crimes tribunal is an international institution," Shattuck said.
He added that Croatia had also said it could not hand over citizens accused of war crimes until it had adopted legislation permitting extradition.
Because Milosevic cooperated over the Dayton peace accord which ended the war in Bosnia, Washington backed the lifting of U.N. sanctions against Yugoslavia.

But, at the insistence of the United States, the Security Council left in place an "outer wall" of sanctions, denying Yugoslavia access to international financial institutions and continuing its Yugoslavia's suspension from U.N. bodies including the General Assembly.
The decision was intended as leverage to speed up Belgrade's cooperation with the tribunal and improve its human rights record. "It is very strong leverage," Shattuck said.
Yugoslavia, saddled with a war-ravaged economy, urgently needs a massive injection of foreign capital.
